title: Single-Aperture Dual-Color Ion Addressing with a DUV-Compatible Bilayer Grating
abstract: Multi-wavelength optical control is a scaling bottleneck for trapped-ion hardware: separate surface emitters consume trap area, interrupt the electrode plane, and expose charge-sensitive dielectric near the ions. Here, a vertically stacked silicon-nitride bilayer routes the $^{40}\text{Ca}^+$ qubit and repump fields-729.4 and 854.2 nm-through one electrode aperture and focuses them $70~μ\text{m}$ above the chip. Three-dimensional FDTDX predicts $0.10~μ\text{m}$ color separation and near-diffraction-limited spots along the ion-chain axis. Multi-level depth-allocation apodization enables this architecture by encoding the coupling envelope in discrete etch levels rather than sub-resolution linewidths. Every feature satisfies a strict $\ge 125\text{ nm}$ deep-UV rule using two etch depths per film. Full-3D Ansys Lumerical simulations independently corroborate directionality, spot size, and repump efficiency. At a common 50 nm reporting grid, the DUV-compatible device matches a 63 nm electron-beam design on the qubit channel (focusing efficiency 0.286 vs 0.288; crosstalk -24.0 vs -24.3 dB). Vertical integration therefore converts wavelength scaling from a lateral-footprint penalty into a layer-allocation problem, providing a pathway toward compact multi-color photonic interfaces for trapped ions and other chip-addressed quantum emitters.
summary: This paper presents a novel approach to overcome the area limitations of multi-wavelength optical addressing in trapped-ion quantum computers. By utilizing a vertically stacked silicon-nitride bilayer grating coupler and employing depth-allocation apodization, the authors successfully co-focus two distinct colors onto a single ion while remaining compatible with standard deep-UV lithography rules. This vertical integration transforms wavelength scaling from a lateral area penalty into a manageable layer allocation problem.
main_problem: Scaling multi-wavelength optical control for trapped-ion quantum computing is bottlenecked by the physical area required for separate surface emitters.
main_result: A vertically stacked SiN bilayer grating coupler successfully co-focuses two widely separated wavelengths onto a single ion while adhering to strict, deep-UV foundry fabrication rules.
method: The authors employ multi-level depth-allocation apodization, encoding the coupling envelope in discrete etch depths rather than relying on minimum feature widths.
model_or_system: The system is a trapped-ion setup using Ca40+ qubits requiring control fields at 729.4 nm and 854.2 nm. The proposed hardware solution is a vertically stacked silicon-nitride bilayer grating coupler integrated over an ion trap.
key_observables: Focusing efficiency, crosstalk (e.g., -24 dB), color separation ($\approx 0.10 \mu	ext{m}$), and the ability to maintain performance comparable to aggressive electron-beam designs.
important_parameters: Wavelengths: 729.4 nm and 854.2 nm; Focusing distance: $70 \mu	ext{m}$; Minimum feature size rule: $\ge 125 	ext{ nm}$.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes the availability of a discrete multi-level (qn) platform with sufficient etch-depth contrast for apodization control.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 3D rendering of the dual-color design, side views of the stratified stack, and comparisons between standard duty-cycle apodization versus the proposed depth-allocation method.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the scaling bottleneck in trapped-ion optics. It then details the novel multi-level depth-allocation grating structure using a SiN bilayer. Performance is validated via 3D FDTD and Lumerical simulations, comparing results against ideal e-beam designs and analyzing focus stability under fabrication tolerances.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware scalability in quantum computing platforms by proposing a photonic integration technique that decouples wavelength scaling from lateral footprint constraints, which is crucial for realizing complex ion trap architectures.

(a) Focusing efficiency of both channels across fabrication tiers: on the 729 nm qubit channel the DUV-clean device is indistinguishable from the e-beam device at the common 50 nm reporting grid (0.288 vs 0.286). (b) 729 nm nearest-neighbor (5 µm) crosstalk, point and 0.5 µm-disk worst case, with a representative single-wavelength benchmark (−30 dB; demonstrated integrated-photonic addressing crosstalk reaches −40 to ≤−50 dB [31, 35]). Figure 5: Trap integration. (a) Trap top view: the outcoupling window sits in the central RF-quiet ground slot, 27 µm off-axis, clear of the RF rails. (b) RF-null radial shift vs. window position from a gapless surface-electrode boundary-element model [36]. The ion is unshifted while the window stays in the field-free ground slot—where a grounded aperture leaves the RF potential unchanged by construction—and the shift rises only when the window is displaced into an RF rail (the computed clearance control).
